parts.title: Part 1 — Renting a holiday cottage
parts.context: A telephone conversation between a lettings agent at Coastline Cottages and a customer enquiring about renting a holiday cottage for her family.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a holiday lettings agent and a woman who wants to rent a cottage for a family holiday. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Good morning, Coastline Cottages, Owen speaking. How can I help you today?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Hi Owen! I'm calling from Bristol—my family and I are hoping to rent a seaside cottage in Cornwall for a week this July.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Lovely choice—Cornwall's gorgeous in July, though bookings are filling fast. Let me start a quick enquiry sheet so I can pull up what's free. May I take your surname, please?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Sure, it's Rachel Kerrigan.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Kerrigan... is that with a C, like C-A-R-R-I-G-A-N?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: No, it starts with a K—K-E-R-R-I-G-A-N.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Got it, thank you, Rachel. All our July rentals run Saturday to Saturday. Which Saturday were you hoping to arrive?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: We were originally looking at Saturday the 12th of July, because that's right when my husband's leave begins.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Ah, let me check the calendar... oh, dear, the week starting the 12th of July is completely sold out across our family-sized cottages—returning guests snapped them up back in January. We do have a few lovely openings the following week, arriving on Saturday the 19th of July.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Hmm, let me think... yes, actually, he has two weeks off, so the 19th of July works even better because the kids will have finished school by then. Let's look at Saturday the 19th.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Brilliant. And how many people will be staying altogether?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: There are six of us in total: my husband and me, my parents, and our two young children—so four adults and two kids.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Lovely, four adults plus two children. Will you be bringing any pets along? Several of our owners welcome dogs, while a few cottages are strictly pet-free.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Yes, we'd love to bring our dog, Milo. He's super house-trained.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Ha, don't tell me he's a giant muddy spaniel who loves jumping on white sofas!

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Definitely not! He's just a tiny terrier—hardly sheds at all, and he sleeps in his own travel crate.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: A small terrier is absolutely fine—most owners adore them. Now, do you have any particular accessibility or layout requirements? A sea-view balcony, maybe, or enclosed garden?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: We don't really care about a balcony, honestly. What is essential, though, is a downstairs bedroom, because my mum had hip surgery last autumn and finds steep cottage staircases really tough.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: That's a very important filter—let me tick ground-floor sleeping right away.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Okay, with those filters on, two great properties pop up for the 19th of July. The first is Harbour View Cottage, right above the old fishing quay.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Oh, that sounds dreamy! What's the weekly rent on Harbour View?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: In peak August it goes up to 940 pounds a week, but since you're arriving in mid-July, your week is 890 pounds.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: That's within our budget. Any catches I should know about? Old stone cottages can have dodgy heating or damp.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Oh, the owners just put in brand-new underfloor heating last winter, so it's super cosy. To be completely upfront, the one drawback is limited parking—it sits on a narrow cobbled lane with space for only one small hatchback, and you're bringing six people, so I guess you might have two cars.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Yes, my parents are driving down separately in their own car, so that could be a headache. What's the second option?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: The second is Meadow Barn, about two miles inland, with a huge gravel driveway that easily fits three vehicles. It's 860 pounds for your week.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Inland sounds peaceful, though the kids will want sand every single day. How far is it from the nearest beach?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: If you fancy a scenic walk along the public footpath, it takes about 25 minutes on foot. Most families drive down with buckets and boards, and it's only 12 minutes by car to Sandy Cove.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Twelve minutes by car is nothing at all! And does Meadow Barn have a decent garden for Milo and outdoor dinners?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: A fully fenced lawn, yes! They used to have a standard gas barbecue out there, actually, though last spring the owners replaced it with a traditional wood-fired oven on the patio—they even leave a stack of dry logs and a pizza peel.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Oh, my kids would lose their minds making homemade pizzas! I think Meadow Barn is the winner. Just before I confirm with my husband, is there a refundable security deposit?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Yes, we hold a security deposit against breakages and refund it within five working days of checkout. For our luxury cottages with hot tubs it's 200 pounds, whereas for Meadow Barn it's 150 pounds.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: That's totally fair. Could you email me the booking link for Meadow Barn and hold it until five o'clock today?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Consider it held until five pm, Rachel. I'll send the link right over.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.instructions: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: Guest surname: {{blank}}
questions.explanation: Khách hàng đính chính họ của mình bắt đầu bằng chữ K chứ không phải chữ C và đánh vần K-E-R-R-I-G-A-N.
questions.evidence: No, it starts with a K—K-E-R-R-I-G-A-N.

distractors.why: Nhân viên đoán nhầm bắt đầu bằng chữ C ('C-A-R-R-I-G-A-N'), nhưng Rachel sửa lại ngay.

questions.prompt: Arrival date: Saturday {{blank}} July
questions.explanation: Tuần bắt đầu ngày 12 tháng 7 đã kín chỗ, nên Rachel đồng ý chọn tuần kế tiếp bắt đầu vào thứ Bảy ngày 19 tháng 7.
questions.evidence: Let's look at Saturday the 19th.

distractors.why: Rachel ban đầu hỏi ngày 12 tháng 7, nhưng nhân viên báo toàn bộ nhà cỡ gia đình tuần đó đã được khách cũ đặt hết từ tháng Giêng.

questions.prompt: Number of adults: {{blank}}
questions.explanation: Đoàn có tổng cộng 6 người, nhưng câu hỏi chỉ hỏi số người lớn ('Number of adults'), tức là 4 người lớn (vợ chồng Rachel và bố mẹ cô).
questions.evidence: There are six of us in total: my husband and me, my parents, and our two young children—so four adults and two kids.

distractors.why: 6 là tổng số khách gồm cả 2 trẻ em, không phải số người lớn.
2 là số trẻ em trong đoàn.

questions.prompt: Pet staying: one {{blank}}
questions.explanation: Rachel khẳng định chú chó Milo của gia đình là giống chó sục nhỏ ('tiny terrier').
questions.evidence: He's just a tiny terrier—hardly sheds at all, and he sleeps in his own travel crate.

distractors.why: Nhân viên nói đùa sợ đó là một chú chó spaniel to lớn hay dính bùn, nhưng Rachel phủ nhận ngay ('Definitely not!').

questions.prompt: Special requirement: a {{blank}} bedroom
questions.explanation: Mẹ của Rachel mới phẫu thuật hông và khó leo cầu thang dốc nên yêu cầu bắt buộc là có một phòng ngủ ở tầng trệt ('a downstairs bedroom').
questions.evidence: What is essential, though, is a downstairs bedroom, because my mum had hip surgery last autumn and finds steep cottage staircases really tough.

distractors.why: Nhân viên gợi ý ban công nhìn ra biển nhưng Rachel nói gia đình không quan tâm đến ban công ('don't really care about a balcony').

questions.evidence: In peak August it goes up to 940 pounds a week, but since you're arriving in mid-July, your week is 890 pounds.

distractors.why: 940 bảng là giá mùa cao điểm tháng 8, không áp dụng cho tuần ngày 19 tháng 7.

questions.evidence: To be completely upfront, the one drawback is limited parking—it sits on a narrow cobbled lane with space for only one small hatchback, and you're bringing six people, so I guess you might have two cars.

distractors.why: Rachel lo nhà đá cũ hỏng hệ thống sưởi, nhưng nhân viên giải thích chủ nhà vừa lắp hệ thống sưởi sàn hoàn toàn mới mùa đông năm ngoái.

questions.prompt: Meadow Barn — Distance to nearest beach: {{blank}} minutes by car
questions.explanation: Đi ô tô từ Meadow Barn ra bãi biển Sandy Cove chỉ mất 12 phút ('only 12 minutes by car').
questions.evidence: Most families drive down with buckets and boards, and it's only 12 minutes by car to Sandy Cove.

distractors.why: 25 phút là thời gian đi bộ dọc lối mòn ('25 minutes on foot'), không phải đi bằng ô tô.

questions.explanation: Chủ nhà đã lắp một lò nướng củi ngoài sân vườn ('traditional wood-fired oven') kèm củi khô và xẻng nướng pizza.
questions.evidence: They used to have a standard gas barbecue out there, actually, though last spring the owners replaced it with a traditional wood-fired oven on the patio—they even leave a stack of dry logs and a pizza peel.

distractors.why: Bếp nướng gas ('gas barbecue') là thiết bị cũ đã bị thay thế từ mùa xuân năm ngoái.

questions.explanation: Tiền đặt cọc bảo đảm hoàn lại trong vòng 5 ngày làm việc cho Meadow Barn là 150 bảng.
questions.evidence: For our luxury cottages with hot tubs it's 200 pounds, whereas for Meadow Barn it's 150 pounds.

distractors.why: 200 bảng chỉ áp dụng cho các căn cao cấp có bồn tắm nước nóng ('luxury cottages with hot tubs').

parts.title: Part 2 — Volunteer orientation at a wildlife park
parts.context: A volunteer coordinator briefing newly accepted weekend volunteers at Cedar Ridge Wildlife Park.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator giving an orientation briefing to new weekend volunteers at Cedar Ridge Wildlife Park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Morning everyone, and a huge welcome to Cedar Ridge Wildlife Park! I'm Tess, the weekend volunteer coordinator. We're thrilled to have twelve new faces joining our conservation team this season. Before we split into zone tours, I want to run through what to pack for your first shift, the perks you'll earn as regulars, and what each park area actually involves.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: First up, gear for your very first shift next Saturday. People always email asking whether they need to buy a high-visibility vest—no need at all, we issue clean hi-vis vests and sun hats at check-in every morning. Likewise, heavy gardening gloves are stocked in the tool shed for everyone to share, so leave yours at home. What you absolutely must bring yourself is a sturdy pair of waterproof walking boots, because paths get muddy fast after rain and we don't keep spare sizes.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: The other essential item to bring in your backpack is a reusable water bottle. We phased out single-use cups across the whole reserve last year, and there are chilled refill taps behind every kiosk. Oh, and someone asked on the registration form about bringing a printed medical certificate—you only ever need one of those if you later apply to train in the venomous reptile house, not for general weekend shifts.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Now, we know you're giving up precious weekends for free, so once you've completed three months of regular shifts, we like to say thank you with a couple of meaningful perks. Just to clarify, our free minibus shuttle from the train station is open to all volunteers from day one, though we can't offer free public bus passes for city routes. After that three-month milestone, however, you receive four complimentary guest tickets each year so your family members can visit the park for free.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: You'll also hear folks joking about a fifty-percent discount in the souvenir shop—sorry to burst that bubble, the staff and volunteer shop discount is twenty percent, though it does cover café lunches too! What volunteers tell us they treasure most at the three-month mark is an invitation to join behind-the-scenes feeding sessions with our keepers once a quarter—watching the red pandas or otters get breakfast up close is unforgettable. And just so expectations are crystal clear, all volunteer shifts remain unpaid even during busy school holidays, although active volunteers do get early notice whenever paid keeper assistant roles open up.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the briefing, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Right, let's look at the six zones where weekend volunteers rotate, and your main duty in each spot. One golden rule across every single zone first: volunteers never touch enclosure gates or check whether latches are locked—only qualified keepers handle animal security, no exceptions.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Let's start down at the Wetland Bird Hide overlooking the reed beds. It's a peaceful post, and your main job there is to greet families at the wooden deck and hand out loan binoculars and laminated spotter sheets so kids can tick off kingfishers and herons.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Next is the Nocturnal Mammal House, where we reverse day and night lighting so visitors can watch owls, bats, and bushbabies active. Even with big warning signs at the door, people constantly forget to switch off their phone settings. So your primary task inside is to stay quietly by the glass and politely remind visitors not to use camera flashes, which startle the animals.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Over at the Children's Petting Barn, things get lively fast with Pygmy goats and guinea pigs. Keepers supervise the brushing and feeding, while volunteers focus on hygiene: every time a school group finishes inside, you guide the children straight out to the outdoor soap and hand-washing stations before they head off to the picnic lawn.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Then there's our Woodland Canopy Trail, which winds through tall cedar trees on raised timber walkways. Because gusts overnight regularly drop pine cones and twigs, volunteers assigned there do an early morning sweep before opening to clear fallen branches from the wooden boardwalks so pushchairs and wheelchairs can roll smoothly.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Down at Penguin Cove, volunteers used to dip thermometers in the pool to record water temperature readings, though automatic digital sensors took over that chore in March. Instead, right after the midday fish feed, you'll assist the keepers in the prep room to weigh and log any daily food leftovers—changes in appetite are often our earliest clue that a bird needs a vet check.

script.speaker: Coordinator
script.text: Finally, on sunny bank-holiday weekends, our Main Entrance Car Park gets jam-packed by ten thirty. Family cars manage fine with the painted arrows, so your chief focus out front is spotting incoming coaches and directing tour buses down to the overflow bays along the south fence so the main entrance stays clear for emergency vehicles. All right, let's grab our name badges and head outside!

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

groups.title: Items volunteers must bring on their first shift
groups.instructions: Choose TWO letters, A–E. Which TWO items must volunteers bring with them on their first shift?

options.text: Waterproof walking boots
A high-visibility vest
Heavy gardening gloves
A reusable water bottle
A printed medical certificate

questions.explanation: Điều phối viên nhấn mạnh tình nguyện viên bắt buộc tự mang giày đi bộ chống nước chắc chắn ('absolutely must bring yourself is a sturdy pair of waterproof walking boots' = A).
questions.evidence: What you absolutely must bring yourself is a sturdy pair of waterproof walking boots, because paths get muddy fast after rain and we don't keep spare sizes.

distractors.why: Áo phản quang (hi-vis vests) được công viên phát sẵn mỗi sáng khi điểm danh.
Găng tay làm vườn dày đã có sẵn trong kho dụng cụ dùng chung nên không cần mang theo.
Giấy khám sức khỏe chỉ cần nếu sau này đăng ký huấn luyện ở khu bò sát có nọc độc, không cần cho ca cuối tuần thông thường.

questions.explanation: Vật dụng thiết yếu thứ hai cần mang trong ba lô là bình nước tái sử dụng ('a reusable water bottle' = D) vì công viên đã bỏ ly dùng một lần.
questions.evidence: The other essential item to bring in your backpack is a reusable water bottle.

groups.title: Benefits offered to regular volunteers
groups.instructions: Choose TWO letters, A–E. Which TWO benefits are offered to volunteers after completing three months of shifts?

options.text: Free public bus passes to the park
Complimentary guest tickets for family members
A fifty-percent discount in the souvenir shop
Behind-the-scenes feeding sessions with keepers
Paid weekend shifts during school holidays

questions.explanation: Sau mốc 3 tháng, tình nguyện viên được tặng 4 vé mời miễn phí mỗi năm để người thân vào tham quan ('four complimentary guest tickets ... family members' = B).
questions.evidence: After that three-month milestone, however, you receive four complimentary guest tickets each year so your family members can visit the park for free.

distractors.why: Công viên có xe đưa đón miễn phí từ ga tàu ngay từ ngày đầu, nhưng không cấp vé xe buýt công cộng miễn phí.
Mức giảm giá ở cửa hàng lưu niệm chỉ là 20%, không phải 50% như lời đùa.
Mọi ca tình nguyện vẫn không có lương kể cả dịp nghỉ học; họ chỉ được báo sớm khi có vị trí tuyển dụng trả lương.

questions.explanation: Quyền lợi thứ hai sau 3 tháng là lời mời tham gia các buổi cho thú ăn hậu trường cùng nhân viên chăm sóc mỗi quý một lần ('behind-the-scenes feeding sessions with our keepers' = D).
questions.evidence: What volunteers tell us they treasure most at the three-month mark is an invitation to join behind-the-scenes feeding sessions with our keepers once a quarter—watching the red pandas or otters get breakfast up close is unforgettable.

groups.title: Volunteer Zones & Key Responsibilities
groups.instructions: What is the main responsibility for volunteers assigned to each area of the wildlife park? Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–H, next to questions 15–20.

options.text: Remind visitors not to use camera flashes
Weigh and log daily food leftovers
Clear fallen branches from wooden boardwalks
Hand out binoculars and spotter sheets
Check that enclosure latches are locked
Direct tour buses to overflow bays
Record water temperature readings
Guide school groups to hand-washing stations

questions.prompt: Wetland Bird Hide
questions.explanation: Tại chòi ngắm chim đầm lầy, nhiệm vụ chính là đón gia đình và phát ống nhòm mượn kèm phiếu nhận diện chim ('hand out loan binoculars and laminated spotter sheets' = D).
questions.evidence: It's a peaceful post, and your main job there is to greet families at the wooden deck and hand out loan binoculars and laminated spotter sheets so kids can tick off kingfishers and herons.

distractors.why: Nguyên tắc chung đã nêu rõ: tình nguyện viên không bao giờ kiểm tra chốt khóa chuồng thú (chỉ nhân viên chuyên môn được làm).

questions.prompt: Nocturnal Mammal House
questions.explanation: Ở khu thú sống về đêm, nhiệm vụ chính là nhắc khách lịch sự không bật đèn flash máy ảnh ('politely remind visitors not to use camera flashes' = A).
questions.evidence: So your primary task inside is to stay quietly by the glass and politely remind visitors not to use camera flashes, which startle the animals.

distractors.why: Không liên quan đến chốt cửa chuồng; tình nguyện viên chỉ đứng bên ngoài kính nhắc khách về ánh sáng.

questions.prompt: Children's Petting Barn
questions.explanation: Nhân viên chăm sóc lo việc cho ăn, còn tình nguyện viên lo vệ sinh bằng cách dẫn các đoàn học sinh ra khu rửa tay có xà phòng ('guide the children straight out to the outdoor soap and hand-washing stations' = H).
questions.evidence: Keepers supervise the brushing and feeding, while volunteers focus on hygiene: every time a school group finishes inside, you guide the children straight out to the outdoor soap and hand-washing stations before they head off to the picnic lawn.

distractors.why: Nhắc tới từ 'feeding' (cho ăn) nhưng việc cho ăn ở chuồng này do nhân viên giám sát, không phải cân thức ăn thừa.

questions.prompt: Woodland Canopy Trail
questions.explanation: Trước giờ mở cửa, tình nguyện viên kiểm tra và dọn cành cây rơi khỏi lối đi lát gỗ ('clear fallen branches from the wooden boardwalks' = C).
questions.evidence: Because gusts overnight regularly drop pine cones and twigs, volunteers assigned there do an early morning sweep before opening to clear fallen branches from the wooden boardwalks so pushchairs and wheelchairs can roll smoothly.

distractors.why: Lối đi trên tán cây không có nhiệm vụ phát ống nhòm.

questions.prompt: Penguin Cove
questions.explanation: Sau bữa ăn trưa của chim cánh cụt, tình nguyện viên hỗ trợ cân và ghi chép lượng thức ăn thừa hằng ngày ('weigh and log any daily food leftovers' = B).
questions.evidence: Instead, right after the midday fish feed, you'll assist the keepers in the prep room to weigh and log any daily food leftovers—changes in appetite are often our earliest clue that a bird needs a vet check.

distractors.why: Bẫy rất điển hình: trước đây tình nguyện viên từng đo nhiệt độ nước ('record water temperature readings'), nhưng từ tháng 3 cảm biến tự động đã thay thế việc này.

questions.prompt: Main Entrance Car Park
questions.explanation: Nhiệm vụ chính ở bãi đỗ xe cổng chính là phát hiện xe khách du lịch và hướng dẫn họ vào khu đỗ dự phòng ('directing tour buses down to the overflow bays' = F).
questions.evidence: Family cars manage fine with the painted arrows, so your chief focus out front is spotting incoming coaches and directing tour buses down to the overflow bays along the south fence so the main entrance stays clear for emergency vehicles.

distractors.why: Không liên quan đến dọn đường gỗ; trọng tâm ở bãi xe là điều phối xe buýt du lịch.

parts.title: Part 3 — Hospitality placement report
parts.context: A hospitality management student, Chloe, meeting her college tutor, Dr. David Patel, to review the draft report on her twelve-week hotel placement.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear a hospitality management student, Chloe, discussing her draft placement report with her tutor, Dr. David Patel. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Come in, Chloe! Good to have you back on campus after twelve weeks at the Harbourside Boutique Hotel. I've gone through your first draft—lots of sharp observations here. Before we dive into edits, I'm curious: you also had an offer from a big international hotel chain, didn't you? What swung your decision?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Yeah, the big chain actually offered a slightly higher monthly training allowance, and it was only ten minutes from my parents' house, whereas the boutique meant a forty-minute bus ride. Still, big chains usually keep trainees pinned to one single desk for the whole twelve weeks. At the boutique, the manager promised I could rotate across reception, wedding events, and housekeeping, and getting that broad departmental mix was what really mattered to me.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Smart long-term thinking. Now, in your reflection log, you mention that month one on reception was pretty stressful. Was that guests turning up early demanding rooms before check-in?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Actually, early arrivals were surprisingly easy once I offered free luggage storage and a coffee voucher, and interns weren't permitted to cover solo night shifts anyway. What nearly drove me round the bend was their ancient booking software—it froze twice a day and required obscure manual keyboard codes just to split a restaurant bill. It took me three solid weeks to stop panicking whenever a queue built up.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Oh, legacy reservation systems—every hospitality graduate has horror stories! I loved the section where you proposed a way to cut breakfast buffet waste. How did the hotel manager react when you pitched it?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: I honestly braced myself for him to shoot it down out of fear that late diners would grumble about smaller portions. Instead, he didn't touch the menu items at all—the head chef kept cooking the exact same dishes—he simply agreed to test my idea of switching to half-sized serving trays during the last thirty minutes for a two-week trial. When food waste dropped by almost a third with zero complaints, he rolled it out permanently.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's gold for your evaluation grade. Now, looking closely at structure, your introduction currently runs to six pages, which makes it heavy. Definitely keep the overview of the hotel's target customer groups—that anchors your marketing section—and your personal learning objectives have to stay because the rubric checks for them. What you really ought to trim out is the two-page architectural history of the Victorian building and its nineteenth-century owners. Interesting as a brochure, yes, but it distracts from a management analysis.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Fair enough, I did get a bit carried away at the local library! And did you get a chance to look at my anonymous staff survey data?

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: I did, and one finding genuinely made me sit up. I wasn't shocked that staff loved the new shift-swapping phone app, and housekeeping actually had an impressive response rate—nearly ninety percent. What truly surprised me was the massive gap between departments on communication: front-desk staff rated daily handovers eight out of ten, while the kitchen brigade rated the exact same process three out of ten!

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the tutorial, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Moving onto section four, I spotted a methodological slip in your financial comparison table. Your room occupancy math checks out fine, and I was pleased you remembered to footnote online travel agency commission fees. The catch is that you've compared the hotel's peak July coastal room rates directly against year-round national averages, which include quiet winter off-peak months—that makes the hotel look artificially profitable.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Oh, of course! Comparing summer peak against annual figures completely skews it. I'll pull the regional Q3 benchmark data instead.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Much stronger. Now, for your final case study on operational problem-solving, you sketched out a double-booking mix-up during a local business conference, though honestly that felt a bit minor to carry a whole section. Were there any bigger incidents you witnessed?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Well, there was a nasty online review from a coach tour group, except the hotel asked me not to quote identifiable guest complaints for confidentiality reasons. The other big one was a Saturday wedding reception for ninety guests when a storm knocked out the power for two hours—reception, chefs, and porters had to switch to gas burners and battery lanterns seamlessly. I'll swap out the conference error and make the wedding power cut my main case study.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Brilliant—that shows cross-department leadership under pressure. One more tip: consider adding two or three short direct quotes from your workplace supervisor. You don't need them to pad out the appendix—you're already close to the word ceiling—and your signed timesheet already proves your hours. What supervisor quotes do is show the marker how realistic your recommendations looked from a management perspective.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: That makes total sense—I have her feedback notes from my exit interview. Speaking of markers, I'm getting pretty nervous about next week's oral presentation.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Really? You're normally great in seminars—is it the Q&A with the external examiner, or worrying the projector will scramble your charts?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Oh, IT tests our slides the day before so I'm calm about the tech, and I actually enjoy answering curveball questions. My real panic is the strict ten-minute cap—when I practised aloud last night, I didn't finish my key findings until minute sixteen!

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Cutting six minutes is totally doable once you drop the building history. Now, with final submission this Friday, what's our next step? Do you need to send the revised draft back to the hotel manager?

script.speaker: Student

Could we possibly squeeze in a quick fifteen-minute chat on Thursday afternoon so you can glance over my rewritten recommendations?

script.speaker: Tutor

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Part 4 — History of public transport ticketing
parts.context: A public lecture by a transport historian tracing how fare collection evolved from nineteenth-century paper tickets to modern contactless payments.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a transport historian giving a lecture on the history of public transport ticketing. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 35.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 35.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good evening. Most of us tap a bank card or phone at a station gate every morning without giving it a second thought. Yet how public transport systems collect fares has always shaped how smoothly cities move. Tonight, I'd like to trace that story across nearly two centuries—from inked ledgers to invisible digital payments.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: When the first passenger railways opened in Britain in the early 1830s, they borrowed their booking method straight from horse-drawn stagecoaches. A clerk behind a wooden counter wrote each traveller's name and destination by hand into a thick paper ledger, then tore off a receipt. Naturally, frustrated passengers sometimes broke into arguments in the booking hall, though the operational nightmare railway bosses actually cared about was the sheer scale of delays at busy stations—trains routinely left twenty minutes late simply waiting for queues to clear.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The breakthrough arrived in 1837 from a quiet stationmaster in northern England named Thomas Edmondson. Edmondson designed a small, stiff pasteboard rectangle pre-printed with departure and arrival stations. He also built a tall wooden cabinet to keep racks of these tickets tidy, while the real technical heart of his invention was a compact wooden press that stamped a unique consecutive serial number onto every single cardboard ticket.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Why did serial numbers matter so much? Certainly, simple arithmetic errors by overworked clerks declined overnight. Far more importantly for railway directors, however, sequential numbering let auditors match the exact number of tickets sold at dusk against the coins in the cash box, dramatically curbing staff fraud—because a clerk could no longer pocket cash from a spare unnumbered slip.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Meanwhile, inside rapidly growing cities, horse-drawn buses and electric trams faced a different puzzle: passengers hopped on and off every few hundred metres. Rather than booking windows, transit operators employed roving conductors who walked up and down the aisle carrying a mechanical bell punch. Each conductor held colour-coded paper slips, punching a tiny hole through specific printed boxes—not to record the vehicle's route, which stayed fixed, but to indicate the fare each rider had paid for their journey.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: By the 1950s and 1960s, rising post-war wages made keeping a conductor on every tram and bus financially unsustainable. While underground networks in London and Paris leaned towards heavy mechanical barriers at station entrances, several central European cities—notably Zurich and Vienna—pioneered a bold alternative: honour-based open boarding, where passengers bought tickets from kerbside machines and compliance was enforced through random inspections carried out by roaming teams of plain-clothes officers.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the lecture, you have some time to look at questions 36 to 40.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 36 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The next major leap came in the late 1960s and 1970s with the arrival of magnetic-stripe paper tickets, trialled heavily on London Underground and San Francisco's BART system. Automated turnstiles could read an encoded iron-oxide strip in a fraction of a second. Occasional tourists often fumbled inserting the thin slips upside down, yet the machines transformed rush hour by allowing station gates to process far higher volumes of commuters than human ticket collectors ever could.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Magnetic stripes weren't without headaches, of course. Today we blame smartphone magnets for wiping hotel keycards, though mobile phones weren't in pockets back in the 1970s. Back then, the main practical drawback of early magnetic tickets was how easily their fragile stripe scratched or lost data whenever riders shoved them loose into a trouser pocket alongside keys or coins.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Engineers solved that wear-and-tear problem in the 1990s by replacing fragile strips with sealed plastic smart cards. Hong Kong led the world when it launched the Octopus card in September 1997, embedding a contactless radio-frequency chip inside durable plastic. Whereas earlier travel passes had to be slid out of protective envelopes for inspection, Octopus readers detected the chip through leather and fabric, enabling busy passengers to breeze through gates without ever removing cards from their wallets.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Over the past decade, we've entered an even simpler era: open-loop payments using everyday contactless bank cards and smartphones. For an occasional visitor, this removes the friction of buying and topping up a local city travel card altogether. Better still, back-office software tracks every tap across buses and trains and automatically applies daily fare capping—meaning riders never need to fill out forms to claim refunds if they take more journeys than planned.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Yet every technological convenience carries a social trade-off. As more transit authorities shut down cash ticket offices completely, consumer advocates raise a valid warning. You don't strictly need a smartphone to ride a modern bus, since physical debit cards work just as well. The deeper risk is that strictly cashless networks exclude elderly residents who prefer paper currency and lower-income people without bank accounts, reminding us that the best ticketing system isn't just the fastest—it has to stay open to everyone. Thank you.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.evidence: Whereas earlier travel passes had to be slid out of protective envelopes for inspection, Octopus readers detected the chip through leather and fabric, enabling busy passengers to breeze through gates without ever removing cards from their wallets.

questions.prompt: Equity concern: Cashless-only systems risk excluding elderly riders and people without bank {{blank}}.
questions.explanation: Mạng lưới hoàn toàn không tiền mặt có nguy cơ gạt ra ngoài người cao tuổi và người thu nhập thấp không có tài khoản ngân hàng ('people without bank accounts').
questions.evidence: The deeper risk is that strictly cashless networks exclude elderly residents who prefer paper currency and lower-income people without bank accounts, reminding us that the best ticketing system isn't just the fastest—it has to stay open to everyone.

distractors.why: Giảng viên giải thích bạn không nhất thiết phải có điện thoại thông minh vì thẻ ghi nợ vật lý vẫn dùng được bình thường.
